text: Setting up a backup policy feels like the job is done, but a policy existing and a backup actually happening are two different claims. This lesson is about checking the second one, not just trusting the first.

A backup job can fail for reasons that have nothing to do with the policy itself — a VM agent that stopped responding, a storage permission change, a snapshot that timed out under load. The policy still looks correctly configured in the portal. The backup it was supposed to produce simply didn't happen, and nothing about the policy's existence tells you that. This is one of the most common, most avoidable causes of real data loss: a job silently failing for weeks, discovered only during an actual restore, at the worst possible moment.

Azure Backup records every attempt as a job with a status like Completed or Failed. This script pulls every job from the last day using a rolling 24-hour window — -From and -To relative to right now — so it always checks yesterday's activity no matter when it actually runs.

Filtering on Status -ne "Completed", rather than specifically matching "Failed", catches anything that didn't finish cleanly — cancelled jobs, jobs stuck in progress too long — not just the one obvious failure mode. Anything caught gets written out as an alert with the workload name and operation, so it's immediately clear what to investigate.

The backup job runs on its own schedule inside Azure Backup — this verification script is deliberately separate, checking on it from the outside. That separation matters: if the check lived inside the same pipeline as the backup, a failure that broke the backup could just as easily break the thing meant to catch it. Running it independently, daily, on its own Azure Automation schedule means a failure is caught within 24 hours.

Next up: automating a simple incident response action — a well-understood, reversible, low-risk step that's genuinely safe to hand to a script, and where the line sits between that and something a human should still decide.
